name: Norethandrolone (Nilevar)

card.summary: One of the first oral anabolic steroids (1950s); documented cholestasis and liver injury ended most use, and only a 1959 weight-gain study speaks to muscle.
card.note: Cholestasis and peliosis hepatis reported in treated patients; withdrawn in many countries in the 1980s.

quick.overview:
Norethandrolone, sold as Nilevar, is an oral 19-nortestosterone steroid synthesized by G. D. Searle in 1953 and introduced as an anabolic steroid in 1956. It was the first anabolic steroid marketed with a favorable separation of anabolic from androgenic effects.

It was prescribed for muscle wasting, burns, trauma and some aplastic anemias. Human data on weight gain come from mid-century studies of underweight patients; it has not been studied for appearance in modern trials.
quick.mechanism: It is an androgen receptor agonist with strong progestogenic activity. Wikipedia reports that aromatase converts it to the potent estrogen ethylestradiol, and that its anabolic-to-androgenic ratio in rodents is about 1:1 to 1:2.
quick.risks: Cholestasis, peliosis hepatis and bile canalicular changes were reported in treated patients in 1959 and 1960 papers. It was withdrawn in many countries in the 1980s over liver concerns, is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, and is reported to be available today only in France.

lead: Norethandrolone (brand names Nilevar and Pronabol) is a synthetic, orally taken androgen and anabolic steroid of the 19-nortestosterone group, a 17α-ethyl derivative of nandrolone. G. D. Searle synthesized it in 1953, initially as a progestin, and introduced it medically as an anabolic steroid in 1956. Wikipedia describes it as the first anabolic steroid marketed with a favorable separation of anabolic and androgenic effects. [1]

It was used for muscle wasting, severe burns, trauma and certain aplastic anemias, and was studied for male hormonal contraception. It was sold in the US in the late 1950s as Nilevar and discontinued there in the 1960s because of limited sales, and was withdrawn in many countries in the 1980s over concerns about liver damage including cholestatic jaundice. [1]

For appearance, the connection is muscle and body weight: as an anabolic steroid it was prescribed to help underweight and wasting patients regain weight and strength, and the same androgen-receptor effect is why bodybuilders and athletes have used compounds of this class to build muscle [1][2]. It is no longer a common product; Wikipedia reports it is available today only in France, and non-medical use is generally illicit [1].

Early clinical papers reported cholestasis and peliosis hepatis in treated patients. [2][3][4] Later, a French randomized trial examined low-dose norethandrolone in elderly acute myeloid leukemia. [5] No modern trials of norethandrolone for appearance have been found. [1]
infobox: Schedule III (US); Schedule IV (Canada); available only in France per Wikipedia

paras: Norethandrolone was used for muscle wasting, severe burns, physical trauma and certain forms of aplastic anemia. [1] A 1959 American Journal of Medicine series evaluated it over six months in underweight persons, with companion papers examining liver function and bromsulphalein retention. [6] A 1967 study reported effects of norethandrolone on the anticoagulant response to bishydroxycoumarin. [7]

Mid-century and later studies explored other uses. A controlled study in patients with chronic renal failure found norethandrolone lowered triglycerides by 50 percent and increased lipoprotein lipase activity, and the authors judged it appropriate for underweight patients [13]. A comparison of five 17-alpha-alkylated steroids including norethandrolone in men with ischaemic heart disease found significant increases in plasma plasminogen activator, and a companion study found most of seven anabolic steroids raised antithrombin III [14][15]. A French cooperative group compared androgens, including high and low doses, in aplastic anaemia [16].

G. D. Searle synthesized norethandrolone in 1953 and first studied it as a progestin alongside norethisterone and noretynodrel, but it was not marketed for that use. In 1955 it was re-examined for testosterone-like activity and found to have anabolic activity similar to testosterone with about one-sixteenth of the androgenic potency [1]. It was introduced medically in 1956 as the first anabolic steroid marketed with a favorable anabolic-androgenic separation, and nandrolone phenylpropionate followed in 1959 [1].

It was launched in the US in the late 1950s as Nilevar and discontinued there in the 1960s because of limited sales; concern about cholestatic jaundice led to withdrawal in many countries in the 1980s [1]. A 1959 JAMA note, a 1959 evaluation in underweight persons and the cholestasis reports of 1959 and 1960 belong to the first wave of clinical literature on the drug [2][6][12].

Norethandrolone is an androgen receptor agonist. Wikipedia states that in rodents its androgenic-to-anabolic ratio is about 1:1 to 1:2, that aromatase converts it to ethylestradiol, and that it has strong progestogenic activity. [1] A 1977 rat liver study found that norethandrolone, unlike norethindrone and ethynyloestradiol, did not cause loss of cytochrome P-450 in vitro. [8]

Wikipedia says the 5-alpha-reduced metabolite binds the androgen receptor less strongly than the parent compound, which may explain the favorable ratio, and that in women its effect on the endometrium resembles that of norethisterone [1]. As a 17-alpha-alkylated steroid it is orally active and hepatotoxic [1].

Papers from 1959 and 1960 reported cholestasis, peliosis hepatis and electron microscopic changes in bile canaliculi in people and rats given norethandrolone. [2][3][9] Wikipedia notes that, as with other 17α-alkylated steroids, long-term high-dose use may cause elevated liver enzymes and cirrhosis. [1]

Wikipedia lists masculinizing effects such as acne, increased hair growth, voice changes and increased sexual desire, and estrogenic effects including fluid retention, breast tenderness and gynecomastia in men. [1] A forensic and rabbit study compared heart lesions in athletes with a history of anabolic steroid abuse to lesions induced by norethandrolone in rabbits. [4]

Wikipedia says it has been used to improve physique and performance and that non-medical use is generally illicit. It is Class C5 in Brazil, Schedule IV in Canada and Schedule III in the US. [1] Analytical work has examined its transformation products in veal feces in the context of boldenone testing. [10]

Wikipedia lists brand names Nilevar and Pronabol, the development code CB-8022 and synonyms including ethylnandrolone and noretandrolone [1]. Forum discussion of the drug is sparse: on T Nation it appears mostly in lists of steroid names, in citations of older studies on progestational activity and in the text of US proposals to list controlled anabolic steroids, where it is named among them [17][18]. Wikipedia reports that it is controlled in many countries, including Schedule III in the US [1].

A 1959 six-month evaluation in underweight persons examined liver function and bromsulphalein retention alongside weight effects. [6] A French randomized phase III trial (NCT00700544, 330 participants, started 2002) in elderly patients with acute myeloid leukemia tested adding androgens, including norethandrolone, after induction therapy; the GOELAMS report found improved survival with androgen addition. [5][11] No studies of norethandrolone for appearance outcomes in healthy people were found.

The GOELAMS trial randomised 330 elderly patients with acute myeloid leukemia after induction chemotherapy and reported improved survival with androgens, including norethandrolone, added to post-remission treatment [5][11]. A 1974 controlled trial studied norethandrolone in chronic renal failure for lipid lowering [13]. Studies of plasma fibrinolytic activity and antiprotease levels in men with ischaemic heart disease examined norethandrolone among several 17-alpha-alkylated steroids [14][15]. A 1986 randomised cooperative trial in aplastic anaemia compared four androgens at different doses [16].

timeline.event: Synthesized by G. D. Searle, initially as a progestin. [1]
Re-examined for testosterone-like activity; anabolic effect similar to testosterone with about one-sixteenth of the androgenic potency. [1]
Introduced medically as an anabolic steroid. [1]
Reports of cholestasis and a six-month evaluation in underweight persons are published. [2][6]

Withdrawn in many countries over liver concerns. [1]

More body mass and strength, as in the 1950s weight-gain studies
angle.text: Norethandrolone was developed as one of the first anabolic steroids with a favorable anabolic-to-androgenic separation and used to help underweight and wasting patients gain weight. Appearance use would run through muscle and body weight; the human data are mid-century weight studies.
